item.title: The Golden Bridge to Monetary Multipolarity
item.description: Gold has overtaken US Treasuries as the world’s top reserve asset because it offers a solution to the challenges of a rogue America. But its renewed relevance also reflects how rapid technological diffusion and increasing dispersion of economic power are creating a more diversified international monetary system.

item.title: Asia’s Natural Disasters Must Not Become Financial Crises
item.description: The dangerous flooding in Nepal and Tibet has demonstrated, once again, the need for prearranged disaster-risk financing to prepare for the economic chain reactions triggered by natural disasters. Asia’s policymakers must act now to help cash-strapped Nepal and strengthen other countries’ resilience before the next crisis hits.

item.title: Is AI Crowding Out Other Investment?
item.description: The AI investment boom has unleashed a wave of demand for capital just as savings are declining and interest rates remain high. As competition for financing intensifies, rising borrowing costs could squeeze non-AI firms looking to finance new factories, equipment, and projects.

item.title: India’s Resilience Depends on Diversified Trade
item.description: India has signed a flurry of trade deals since Donald Trump’s return to the White House in an attempt to ensure that no single bilateral rupture will cause catastrophic harm. It should continue to expand its trade ties, while being wary of any bilateral agreement that curtails its freedom of action vis-à-vis third countries.

item.title: Whipsaw Trade Policy Is Depressing Foreign Direct Investment
item.description: If a country opts for higher trade restrictions to promote its perceived domestic interests, a predictable policy is far superior to a volatile one. As new research shows, uncertainty causes unnecessary and large collateral damage to FDI inflows.

item.title: Why the Far Right’s War on Modern Architecture Matters
item.description: The Alternative for Germany’s fixation on architecture is more revealing than it may seem. Cultural policy is not only one area where the party can actually change conditions on the ground at the state level; it is also intimately tied to far-right forces’ exclusionary political agenda.

item.title: How Will the US-Iran War End?
item.description: The latest US effort to subdue Iran—an "economic D-Day" intended to cut off the Islamic Republic from the world economy—can’t succeed without the support of the country’s biggest trade partner. The only stable solution to the impasse in the Gulf is one that involves China and increases economic integration in the region.

item.title: Germany’s Political Firewall Is Crumbling
item.description: The upcoming election in Saxony-Anhalt could give the far-right Alternative für Deutschland control of a state government for the first time in Germany’s postwar history. Its rise offers a crucial lesson for democracies elsewhere: closing ranks against extremist parties is no substitute for effective governance.

item.title: The Swimmable City Test
item.description: In committing to provide a safe swimmable place within 15 minutes of every home by 2035, London Mayor Sadiq Khan has set a measurable, time-bound goal that cannot be met through a single program or line item on the budget. Instead, it requires a public mission capable of mobilizing all ministries and shaping markets.

item.title: The Tale of Economics
item.description: A new book tells the story of the economics discipline and its original purpose with a degree of verve and imaginativeness that puts dreary mainstream economists to shame. In the process, it gets at fundamental truths that major schools within the discipline have managed to obscure.

item.title: AI’s Market Path Will Get Bumpier
item.description: By enhancing the input that goes into so much of what we do—intelligence—AI’s potential to drive higher economic growth is enormous. But with fears of the technology's unintended consequences affecting the pace and depth of adoption, the promise of long-term gains must be set against more immediate risks.

item.title: American Götterdämmerung
item.description: US President Donald Trump and his Treasury secretary’s latest desperate threats confirm how much American power has waned on their watch. Far from compelling others to join their efforts to isolate Iran, they are hastening the transition to a post-American world order.

item.title: Hard Lessons for Europe From the Ceuta Crisis
item.description: European Union leaders should have received several messages during the recent surge of migrants into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. In particular, cohesion without trust is fragile; dependence without limits leads to vulnerability; and selective enforcement of international law risks eroding a pillar of Europe’s strategic identity.

item.title: The World’s Silent Majority for International Cooperation
item.description: The hollowing out of global institutions has resulted in a rapid loss of credibility for the international rule of law. But a majority of people worldwide still recognize the value of multilateralism, which countries can preserve in the absence of superpower consent by finding better ways to cooperate.

item.title: Building Canada’s Post-American Economy
item.description: Canada’s dependence on the US market has become a strategic liability, leaving it vulnerable to President Donald Trump’s bullying. Reducing that dependence will require building industries that can compete globally while removing the structural barriers that prevent innovative Canadian firms from scaling.

item.title: Trump and Xi Should Align on AI
item.description: When potential outcomes are systemic and irreversible, preparation must precede certainty. This is the logic behind insurance, as well as every pandemic plan and arms-control treaty ever created, and it must be the principle that guides our approach to AI—beginning at the upcoming US-China summit.

item.title: The Quiet Revolution in Services
item.description: While economists debate whether industrialization can still play its traditional growth-promoting role in the current global and technological context, services have unexpectedly become an engine for economic development around the world. For developing and developed economies alike, the timing could not be better.

item.title: AI Addicts Won’t Make Better Workers
item.description: Economists widely agree that AI will boost labor productivity. But this view does not account for the possibility that hyperscalers will go all out to get people hooked on LLMs, because the narrower applications for which these tools are actually useful do not justify the massive investments made so far.

item.title: Latin America’s Crime Tax
item.description: Even excluding lives lost, communities displaced, and families ravaged, the economic costs of organized crime in the region produce a bleak picture, shaving 0.5–2 percentage points off annual GDP growth in the most affected countries. That, too, represents a hefty human toll.

item.title: Are The Walls Closing in on Bessent?
item.description: Far from suggesting financial Armageddon, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s futile efforts to keep a lid on Treasury yields suggest that, once again, the dollar is America’s currency, but everyone else’s problem. But while investors have few alternatives, the bond-salesman-in-chief cannot be complacent.
